answer.evidence: This is a wooden stairwell tile seen from above and in front. The dark pit and descending steps (rows 20-38) are horizontal tread surfaces. Dark riser lines at rows 34 and 38 and the alternating tread and riser bands in rows 30-38 mark front-edge lines and shadows. The railing at rows 10-19 stands at the back, and the wooden side walls at the left and right (about 3 px wide) show receding sides. The riser bands (rows 30-38) and the lower landing (rows 39-42) give a front face of 3 or more rows, so it is not a flat slab. The stair-edge lines are the only clear top-surface evidence, so this reading is moderately confident.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small wooden stairwell. With the kind mismatch and the shallow wood texture, and no clear evidence it matches the Beodeul bar, it fails.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small wooden stair-down piece, which is a reasonable ground-kind prop even though the references are grass and paving. It measures 7 visible tones per tile, equal to the paving reference and well above the grass reference's 3. Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references. Only 1% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outlines lean brown and read as the dark tone of the adjacent wood rather than a black sticker line. The weak point is texture: it has only 10 colours in total and little visible wood grain, so the treads read as fairly clean banded planks. That is still comparable to the paving reference, which also uses only 7 colours. On the primary facts it holds up against the references, so I pass it, with a note that the grain is modest.
